Trying to Conceive

When to try for pregnancy again after stillbirth

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

After a stillbirth, you may want another pregnancy soon, need more time or feel uncertain about ever trying again. There is no waiting period that fits every family. The useful question is what needs to be checked or treated before you try, alongside what feels manageable for you. Research about the interval after stillbirth can inform that conversation, but it cannot give personal medical clearance or promise a particular outcome.

Be clear about the loss and the interval being discussed

This guide concerns conception after a baby died before or during birth and was born without signs of life. Definitions of stillbirth use different gestational thresholds in different countries. A baby who was born alive and died in the first day had a neonatal death; the cause and the parent’s recovery still matter, but the stillbirth interval studies below do not directly answer every question after neonatal death.

An interpregnancy interval describes the gap from the end of one pregnancy to the start of the next. It is not the age gap between two births. Ask your clinician which interval they mean and whether their advice comes from stillbirth research, general pregnancy-spacing guidance, or a particular problem in your own medical history.

What the stillbirth studies actually found

A 2019 study followed 14,452 subsequent births after stillbirth in Finland, Norway and Western Australia. Compared with a gap of 24–59 months, intervals under six months or of six to eleven months were not associated with increased odds of another stillbirth, preterm birth or a baby being small for gestational age. A 2023 California study of 5,581 pregnancies after stillbirth also found no increase in its measured adverse outcomes with shorter intervals, including under three months.

Both studies used existing records rather than assigning people to a waiting period. Differences between families can affect the results, and rare outcomes are difficult to assess precisely. These findings do not establish that every short interval is safe, that three months is an ideal target, or that waiting six or twelve months prevents recurrence. RCOG advises balancing physical and psychological considerations; broad spacing advice needs to be interpreted alongside the circumstances of your loss.

Physical recovery can create a reason to wait

Your body still needs postpartum care after a stillbirth. Review bleeding, pain, wounds, anemia after blood loss, infection, blood pressure and any ongoing illness with your maternity team. A calendar date or the return of a period does not show that all these issues have resolved. Arrange the follow-up you were offered and seek earlier assessment for new or worsening symptoms instead of waiting for a routine appointment.

A previous cesarean or other surgery on the uterus needs a specific discussion. Shorter intervals after cesarean have been associated with uterine rupture during a later labor and other maternal complications. The reassuring stillbirth cohort findings do not replace advice about your scar, the operation, or future birth options. Ask what recovery milestone or treatment goal underlies a recommendation to delay and when it should be reviewed.

Find out whether pending results would change the plan

Placental examination, tests during the admission, genetic testing and a postmortem, if you chose one, may help explain the loss. They can sometimes identify a condition needing treatment or genetic advice before another pregnancy. A postmortem is a broader examination than a single biopsy, and it requires consent. Results can also remain inconclusive; an unanswered question does not mean that you caused the loss.

Ask which results are still pending, when they are expected and whether they could change what you do before conception. An interim appointment may help if the final review is delayed. Waiting for a particular result can be useful, but every family does not need the same test or the same waiting period. Agree a plan with the team rather than assuming that you must obtain a complete explanation before you can discuss trying again.

Fertility may return before a period

Ovulation can happen before the first period after birth, so lack of a period is not contraception. Postpartum guidance warns that pregnancy can occur from about three weeks after birth. This is a reason to plan protection if needed, not a prediction that you personally will ovulate then or that it is the right time to conceive. The first period does not reliably arrive in a particular week after a stillbirth.

Bleeding and discharge as the uterus recovers, called lochia, can continue for several weeks and may be difficult to distinguish from a returning period. The amount and color should generally settle, but a fixed day-by-day color chart cannot confirm recovery. Discuss contraception before resuming sex if you want to wait; the suitable method and when it becomes effective depend on your health and the postpartum stage.

Intimacy and readiness may need separate conversations

Wanting another pregnancy does not necessarily mean being ready for sex, and wanting closeness does not necessarily mean wanting conception. Pain, dryness, tiredness and the emotional meaning of sex after the loss can all affect intimacy. Ask your clinician about recovery before intercourse, especially if bleeding, pain or a wound remains; do not push through painful penetration.

Partners can reach different decisions at different times. Talk about what each of you feels able to manage, without using a deadline to pressure the other person. A midwife, doctor or bereavement counselor can help if pain, fear or disagreement is making the conversation difficult. You can revisit the decision, choose temporary contraception or decide not to try again.

Make space for grief and mental health care

Physical healing and emotional adjustment rarely follow the same timetable. Wanting another pregnancy soon does not mean you loved your baby less, and waiting does not mean that you have given up. A new pregnancy is not a treatment for grief. Support can help you consider the decision while continuing to remember your baby.

Tell your clinician if persistent low mood, panic, intrusive memories or difficulty functioning is affecting daily life. Ask about bereavement support and assessment for depression or trauma-related symptoms where appropriate. You do not need to prove that all sadness has ended before discussing pregnancy, but untreated symptoms and your available support deserve attention in the plan.

Review medicines without stopping antidepressants yourself

If you take an antidepressant or another regular medicine, arrange a review before trying. Some antidepressants can be used in pregnancy, and decisions depend on the medicine, previous response and the benefits and risks for you. The aim is a plan that supports your health during a future pregnancy, rather than an assumption that stopping treatment is always safer.

Do not abruptly stop an antidepressant or change the dose on your own. Sudden stopping can cause withdrawal symptoms, and any planned reduction should be agreed with the prescriber. Include nonprescription medicines and herbal products in the review. If you become pregnant before this appointment, contact the prescribing clinician promptly and keep taking prescribed treatment unless they advise a change.

Start practical preparation when conception becomes a possibility

Take folic acid before trying and through the first twelve weeks of pregnancy. NHS guidance recommends 400 micrograms daily for most people and a prescribed higher dose for certain medical or pregnancy histories. Ask which dose is appropriate for you, especially if a previous pregnancy involved a neural tube defect or you have diabetes or take relevant medicines. Folic acid supports early development; it does not guarantee that a stillbirth will not recur.

Ask for help to stop smoking and avoid alcohol while trying to conceive. Review existing conditions, nutrition and any recommended vaccinations with your clinician. These are supportive steps for the next pregnancy, not an explanation of why your baby died. If you are already pregnant, begin the recommended folic acid promptly and arrange care rather than feeling that you have missed the opportunity to prepare.

Include age and fertility treatment in an individual decision

Age, general health and a history of difficulty conceiving can affect the balance between waiting and trying. If your baby was conceived with fertility treatment, ask your fertility and maternity teams to review the loss together when possible. A consultation can explore recovery, what the results mean and what options may remain without committing you to another treatment cycle.

Ask the clinic directly about timing, eligibility, stored embryos if relevant, costs and the chance of success in your circumstances. Neither a previous conception nor a waiting period guarantees another pregnancy or a healthy birth. It is reasonable to consider the emotional and practical burden, seek support, pause treatment or decide against further treatment. Age-related concerns deserve a timely discussion, but should not erase a medical reason to allow recovery.

Leave with a plan you can revisit

Before trying, ask your team to identify any condition requiring treatment, any result worth waiting for, the recommended contraception while you wait, and who to contact when you have a positive test. If a delay is advised, ask its purpose and when the decision can be reassessed. If you conceive sooner than planned, seek early maternity care; a short interval is not proof that something will go wrong.

During recovery, get urgent medical help for heavy bleeding, fever, foul-smelling discharge or worsening pain. Severe abdominal pain, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or heavy bleeding with weakness needs emergency assessment. Seek immediate help if you feel unable to keep yourself safe. These symptoms need care now; they should not be left for a future pregnancy-planning visit.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Separate stillbirth-specific observational interval findings from general spacing guidance and individual surgical or medical risks.

Discuss recovery, pending investigations, emotional readiness, contraception and preconception care together.

Keep medicine changes supervised and give urgent postpartum symptoms immediate attention.

How BeMama can help

Use the planning appointment to identify what needs to happen before trying, why any delay is suggested and when to review the decision.

When to seek help

Seek urgent care for heavy bleeding, fever, foul discharge or worsening pain; severe pain, chest pain, breathing difficulty, fainting, heavy bleeding with weakness or inability to stay safe needs immediate help. Do not abruptly stop prescribed antidepressants.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • There is no single evidence-based waiting period that suits everyone after stillbirth.
  • Observational studies of stillbirth intervals are reassuring but cannot provide individual clearance.
  • Recovery, cesarean scars, pending results, health and personal readiness may change the timing.
  • Fertility can return before a period; arrange contraception if you wish to wait.
  • Review medicines and folic acid before trying, and do not stop antidepressants abruptly.

Frequently asked questions

How many months should I wait after a stillbirth?

There is no universal three-, six- or twelve-month answer. Stillbirth-specific studies did not find higher measured risks with shorter intervals, but recovery, an operation, ongoing illness or pending results can justify waiting in an individual case. Make the decision with your maternity team and revisit any recommended delay.

Does waiting at least six months prevent another stillbirth?

No waiting period guarantees prevention. Time can help you recover or complete treatment, but the evidence does not establish a universal six-month rule after stillbirth. Ask what problem a proposed delay is intended to address rather than treating the number alone as protection.

Should I wait for postmortem or genetic results before trying?

Sometimes the results may change treatment or lead to genetic counseling, so waiting can help. Ask which result could affect your plan and when it is expected. A full explanation is not always found, and results review and timing should be individualized rather than made a compulsory identical process for everyone.

When will I be fertile again after a stillbirth?

Ovulation may return before your first period. Pregnancy is possible within weeks after birth, but the timing varies and a particular week cannot be predicted for you. Use suitable contraception if you want to wait; fertility returning does not mean that recovery is complete.

Do I need a different plan after a cesarean?

Yes, discuss the operation and uterine scar with your obstetrician. Shorter intervals can matter for later maternal risks, particularly labor after cesarean. Stillbirth interval studies should not be used to override advice based on your surgery and future birth plan.

Should I stop my antidepressant before trying?

Do not stop it suddenly or change the dose yourself. Ask your prescriber to review the medicine, your mental health history and pregnancy plans. Some antidepressants can be used in pregnancy, and the benefits and risks need an individual discussion.

What if my partner and I feel ready at different times?

Different timelines are common. Talk about recovery, grief, intimacy and what support would help, without pressuring either person. Bereavement counseling can help you discuss the decision. It is valid to wait, reconsider or decide not to have another pregnancy.

What if I am already pregnant sooner than advised?

Contact your maternity team and prescriber promptly for early care and a review of the reasons for the earlier advice. Continue prescribed medicines unless a clinician advises a change. A short interval does not mean that harm is inevitable, and you deserve supportive care without blame.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
